correctness.rationale: The sum of the two maxima is the maximum over all products of a signed coordinate and an ordered-pair slope. Equality occurs exactly when both separate maxima are attained. For a nonconstant boundary point the anchor and tight-edge sets are nonempty and L>0. By finiteness, the inactive inequalities are strict along all sufficiently small segments in the nullspace of the active rows, making its nullity exactly the face dimension. Comparing all active-pair rows first with one edge fixed and then with one anchor fixed gives a common r=sign(f_i) h_i at all anchors, and slope change -r on all oriented tight edges. Consequently h_i+(r/L)f_i is a constant c_C on each component. A positive anchor fixes c_C=r/L, a negative one fixes c_C=-r/L, and both signs together force r=0; no anchor gives an independent offset. These relations suffice for all active rows and yield exactly u+epsilon. The constants ±1 are extreme by coordinatewise equality in the sup-norm bound; interior points are not extreme and the singleton case is an interval. Scanning all pairs and traversing the tight graph is quadratic in arithmetic operations and comparisons, not a bit-complexity or floating-point guarantee.
residual_risks: The packaged checker short-circuits constant functions at lines 43–44 and its returned second component there is not the constant point's face dimension; the 46,000-case count is not 46,000 independent rank checks on all boundary types. The stated dimension formula is only for nonconstant points, and the constant endpoints are proved separately.

checked_sources: Frozen Finding and proof, including the disconnected extreme example
value.rationale: The criterion addresses a natural finite sum-norm extremality problem where the motivating literature supplies exact examples but local saturation alone is insufficient. The graph invariant detects both unanchored degrees of freedom and an independent global slope degree of freedom, yielding all minimal-face dimensions by an O(|S|^2) scan and traversal instead of forming and ranking product constraints. It also explains why a disconnected tight graph can support an extreme point. This all-face, arbitrary-metric calculation is useful independently of the discrete grid problem.
residual_risks: No claim of efficient enumeration of all extreme points, infinite-space applicability, or robustness of numerical tightness detection.
